extraction.research_question: Can individual state legislators' lawmaking effectiveness be measured comparably across 97 state legislative chambers and over time, and does the measure validly capture effectiveness? Two illustrative questions follow: (1) how does the majority-party advantage in lawmaking vary with ideological polarization, majority-party cohesion, and seat-share imbalance? (2) how do institutional designs (pay, professionalism, session length, staff, agenda-control and gatekeeping rules, committee-appointment votes, chamber size, term limits) shape the relative lawmaking power of majority vs minority, chairs vs rank-and-file, and senior vs freshman legislators? (pp. 21-22, 30-34)
extraction.theory: Effectiveness is defined as 'the proven ability to advance a member's agenda items through the legislative process and into law' (Volden and Wiseman 2014, quoted p. 22). It is measured across lawmaking stages, with later and rarer stages weighted more heavily (pp. 22-23). Study 1 draws on conditional party government (Aldrich and Battista 2002): polarization and majority cohesion should raise majority advantage. A competing electoral account says tenuous majorities intensify partisanship (Rosenthal 1998). Median-voter logic predicts moderates do better (Black 1958; Downs 1957; Hitt, Volden and Wiseman 2017). Study 2 is explicitly exploratory with no specific hypotheses; it draws on Anzia and Jackman (2013) for agenda and gatekeeping effects (pp. 30-34).
extraction.data: Sample: 80,344 legislator-term SLES scores across 1,032 chamber-terms (legislative sessions) in 97 state legislative chambers, 1987-2018, built from about 1.8 million bills (p. 21). Kansas is excluded because sponsor names are rarely attached to bills (fn. 1, p. 22). Four states enter after 2003 (MA 2009; NE, OR, RI 2007). Unit for Table 1: legislator-term (72,888 observations with full covariates; 53,846 lower-chamber and 19,042 upper-chamber). Unit for Tables 2 and 3: chamber-term (868 and 874 chamber-terms in Table 2; 776-818 in Table 3). Sources: state government online legislative archives (bill histories and sponsors), LexisNexis and NewsBank newspaper coverage (substantive significance), Shor and McCarty (2011) ideal points (coverage 1993-2016), Anzia and Jackman (2013) procedural rules, and North Carolina NCCPPR rankings for 2005-2012 (Edwards 2018).
extraction.method:
Measure: a weighted average of 15 indicators. These are the shares of a legislator's bills that reach each of five stages (introduced, action in committee, action beyond committee, passed home chamber, became law) at each of three significance levels (commemorative weight 1, substantive weight 5, substantive and significant weight 10). Scores are normalized so each chamber-term has mean 1 (Eq. 1, pp. 23-24). Validity checks: hand-coding audit, North Carolina criterion validation, and construct validation via lagged correlations and OLS. Table 1 is OLS with fixed effects by term and chamber (or state), with standard errors clustered by legislator. Tables 2 and 3 are chamber-level OLS with standard errors clustered by state chamber. Outcomes are the median majority-minus-minority SLES gap, the share of majority members above the minority median, and median differences for chairs vs rank-and-file and non-freshmen vs freshmen. Tests are two-tailed (+p<0.1, *p<0.05, **p<0.01).</method>
<parameter name="identification">No causal identification strategy. Results are associational. Fixed effects absorb state, chamber and term differences. The authors state that endogeneity is unaddressed: rules may be chosen by strong parties, and term limits or professionalism may respond to entrenched power (p. 34). Study 2 is framed as illustrative and exploratory.
extraction.scope: Population: state legislators in 97 chambers (49 states, derived from Kansas exclusion and Nebraska's unicameral chamber), 1987-2018. Institution: state legislatures only. The paper says SLES values should not be compared directly across chambers or eras, because absolute scores are relative to each chamber-term; comparisons of factor effects across settings are appropriate (pp. 23-24). It explicitly does not capture oversight, obstruction, constituency service, or behind-the-scenes lawmaking (fn. 8, p. 24).

key_findings.finding: Hand-coding audit of the bill-coding pipeline: research assistants found 46,693 of 49,037 sampled bills (95.2%) accurately coded; after fixes, alignment exceeded 99%.
Criterion validity: SLES tracks North Carolina's subjective NCCPPR effectiveness rankings and outperforms hit-rate metrics.

key_findings.finding: Seniority, chairs, and majority status predict higher SLES in the pooled OLS (Model 1.1).
key_findings.numbers: Seniority 0.032 per term (about 3% of mean 1); Committee chair 0.507; Majority party 0.370, which is 58% above the minority mean of 0.636 (p. 26)

key_findings.finding: Study 1: polarization and majority-party cohesion widen the majority advantage (conditional party government).
key_findings.numbers: Polarization 0.158 (SLES gap, p<0.05) and 0.072 (share more effective, p<0.01); 1 SD (0.48) increase in polarization gives +0.075 gap and +3.5 points; majority heterogeneity -0.886 and -0.347 (p<0.01); 1 SD decline gives +0.10 gap and +4.0 points

key_findings.finding: Study 1: insecure majorities raise partisanship. Smaller seat-share imbalance widens the majority SLES advantage, the reverse of the expectation for insecure majorities.
key_findings.numbers: Partisan Seat Share Imbalance -0.529 (p<0.01) on SLES gap and -0.168 (p<0.01) on share; Arkansas (imbalance 0.49) vs Colorado (0.03) implies a 0.24-point larger SLES gap in Colorado (Model 2.1)

key_findings.finding: Study 1: professionalism, gatekeeping and calendar control correlate with a larger majority advantage. Other covariates were weaker.
key_findings.numbers: Legislative professionalism 0.693 (gap, p<0.01) and 0.351 (share, p<0.01); Majority Party Controls Calendar 0.128 and 0.058 (p<0.05); Committee Gatekeeping 0.128 (gap, p<0.05)

key_findings.finding: Study 2: session length and majority-party calendar control favor majority and chairs over others. Session length raises the majority and chair gaps, and in the freshman-seniority gap it is not significant.
key_findings.numbers: Log Session Length 0.179 (Partisan Difference, p<0.01) and 0.206 (Chair Difference, p<0.01); Majority Party Controls Calendar 0.116 (p<0.05) on partisan gap

key_findings.finding: Study 2: staff per legislator narrows the chair gap; chamber votes on committee appointments narrow the chair gap; larger chambers widen the chair gap.
key_findings.numbers: Staff per Legislator -0.020 (chair gap, p<0.05); Chamber Votes on Committee Appointments -0.180 (chair gap, p<0.01); Log Chamber Size 0.205 (chair gap, p<0.05)

key_findings.finding: Study 2: higher pay and longer sessions are associated with a smaller seniority gap among freshmen-vs-senior majority members; term limits show negative coefficients in the first three columns.
key_findings.numbers: Log Annual Salary -0.032 (majority seniority gap, p<0.01) and -0.026 (minority, p<0.05); Log Session Length -0.071 (minority seniority gap, p<0.01); Term Limits -0.094 (majority seniority gap, p<0.1); Polarization -0.084 (minority seniority gap, p<0.01)

key_findings.finding: Majority-party and chair advantages are sensitive to design choices. The authors interpret the institutional results as incumbents and chairs keeping control.

limitations: Results are associational. The authors say the institutional-design relationships may face endogeneity (rules chosen by strong parties; term limits or professionalism adopted to weaken entrenched politicians) (p. 34).
Study 2 is explicitly exploratory, with no specific hypotheses tested (p. 34).

Effectiveness excludes oversight, voting for district interests, communication, and obstruction; it also misses behind-the-scenes lawmaking and bills that hitchhike on must-pass legislation (pp. 22, 24, fn. 8).
Absolute SLES values are not comparable across chambers or eras; only relative comparisons of factor effects are recommended (pp. 23-24).

Sponsor attribution for committee bills and multiple-sponsor bills required judgment (fn. 2, p. 22), and some states (Massachusetts by-request bills, Connecticut, Iowa, Idaho committee bills) required case-by-case decisions (p. 23-24).
Substantive significance is coded from newspaper mentions and state-specific dictionaries (p. 23), with a coding error rate of 4.8% before revision (p. 24).
SLES and NCCPPR rankings may tap different concepts; party leaders who act behind the scenes may be underrated by SLES (p. 24).
Caution is urged about women and minority coefficients, which may reflect unmodeled factors (p. 26).
About 8,000 Table 1 observations are lost to missing covariates, and Nebraska's 301 observations are dropped as nonpartisan (fn. 9, p. 25).
Term limits are a binary indicator; binding status and length are not modeled in the main text (fn. 20, p. 34; Table A9 in appendix).
Kansas is excluded for data quality (fn. 1, p. 22).

summary_md:
Bucchianeri, Volden and Wiseman adapt the congressional Legislative Effectiveness Score to state legislatures. The result is the SLES: 80,344 legislator-term scores across 97 chambers, 1987-2018, built from about 1.8 million bills. Each score is a weighted average of 15 indicators: the share of a member's sponsored bills that reach each of five stages (introduced, action in committee, action beyond committee, passed chamber, law), at three significance levels weighted 1, 5 and 10. Scores are normalized to mean 1 within each chamber-term. The authors stress that absolute scores should not be compared across chambers or eras.

They check validity three ways. A hand audit found 95.2% of 49,037 sampled bills correctly coded. In North Carolina (2005-2012), SLES alone explains about half the variance in subjective effectiveness rankings and beats simple hit rates. Scores also persist from term to term (rho 0.38-0.66, highest when majority control does not change). In pooled OLS, majority status adds 0.370 (0.362 lower chamber, 0.387 upper) and a committee chair adds 0.507 (0.609 lower vs 0.307 upper). Moderates are more effective. Two exploratory chamber-level studies find that majority advantage grows with polarization, majority-party cohesion and professionalism. All results are associational.

What this means for Paul's system: the paper is the direct method source for the unactivated effectiveness shadow (fec/engine/legislative_effectiveness.py), which copies the five stages, the 1/5/10 weights and per-chamber-term normalization. The shadow departs from SLES in two ways: it credits cosponsors, and it measures significance by CU mention frequency. The paper's validation evidence therefore does not carry over to those changes. The paper also exposes three weak spots in the live rank:
- Leg% and Influence% are pooled across the House and Senate.
- The efficiency term is the hit-rate kind of measure the paper outperforms.
- Nothing controls for majority status, which the paper finds is the largest structural driver of advancement.

The brain already records that CEL LES is roughly orthogonal to the live score (+0.10 Spearman).

bearings.paper_claim: SLES is a weighted average of 15 indicators: five stages (BILL, AIC, ABC, PASS, LAW) times three significance classes (commemorative 1, substantive 5, substantive and significant 10), normalized so each chamber-term has mean 1 (Eq. 1). Window: 97 chambers, 1987-2018; unit: legislator-term (80,344). Validity: a coding audit found 46,693 of 49,037 sampled bills (95.2%) correct, over 99% after fixes. In North Carolina (2005-2012), SLES explains about half the variance in NCCPPR rankings and outperforms hit rates.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 22-24, Eq. 1; Validity Explorations p. 24; Figure 1
bearings.system_side: The shadow uses the same five stages and the 1/5/10 impact classes (other values become unknown). It normalizes 'N/5 per originating chamber and Congress' with a sponsor mean-one reference, normalizes each chamber-term before applying the 0.8 Congress decay, and uses within-chamber percentiles. It departs from SLES in four ways: it credits cosponsors (role weights 3/2/1) with 2^(-delay/180) timing decay, it treats letters as substantive (weight 5), it takes significance from CU and trade-association mention frequency rather than newspaper coverage, and it offers a 70/30 advocacy composite. Status: shadow candidate, not activated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The stage and weight structure transfers. The paper is the state adaptation of the congressional Volden-Wiseman (2014) LES, and the shadow scores the U.S. Congress. The paper's validation evidence (coding audit, North Carolina criterion, persistence) covers only sponsor-based SLES with newspaper-coded significance, so it does not validate the cosponsor credit, timing decay, CU-mention significance or 70/30 composite. Those adaptations remain UNVERIFIED until checked against CEL LES for the same members and Congresses.

bearings.paper_claim: In North Carolina 2005-2012, SLES tracks subjective effectiveness rankings better than hit-rate metrics (share of sponsored bills that pass). Absolute scores are relative to each chamber-term and should not be compared across chambers. Majority status adds 0.370 SLES (UNSTRATIFIED pooled estimate; strata: 0.362 lower, 0.387 upper), 58% above the minority mean of 0.636.
bearings.paper_location: p. 24 and Figure 1; pp. 23-24 (comparability); Table 1, p. 26-27
bearings.system_side: Live efficiency is a hit rate: per category, the decay-weighted signed count of advanced sponsored or original-cosponsored bills divided by total decay weight. It is scaled by the cross-member maximum and percentile-ranked across all 533 members, pooling the House and Senate. Leg% is then computed in 'legacy' mode over the same pooled roster. Nothing adjusts for majority or minority status.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The North Carolina criterion covers one state chamber pair over 8 years. Applying it to Congress assumes chamber structure plays the same role, which Volden-Wiseman's congressional work supports qualitatively. The finding argues for within-chamber normalization and a stage-weighted measure over a hit rate. It does not show that the CU-signed agenda term is invalid, because that term measures topical advocacy, not general effectiveness.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/moneyball-rank-pillars#Legislative pillar (stance-gated agenda plus efficiency)|Legislative pillar (stance-gated agenda plus efficiency)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Committee chairs score 0.507 SLES above rank-and-file (UNSTRATIFIED pooled estimate; strata: 0.609 lower chamber vs 0.307 upper). The chair gap widens with chamber size (Log Chamber Size 0.205 on the chair difference, p<0.05) and narrows where the chamber votes on committee appointments (-0.180). Majority status adds 0.370 (strata 0.362 / 0.387).
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 (p. 27), Figure 6 (p. 30); Table 3 (p. 35)
bearings.system_side: Leadership multipliers are the same in both chambers: Chair 3.0 full / 7.5 sub, Ranking 2.0 / 4.5, Vice 1.0 / 2.0. Influence% = committee_raw / max across all 533 members, so the House and Senate are pooled. The minority Ranking member gets two-thirds of the Chair multiplier, and there is no majority-status term.
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are associational state-legislature estimates and are not causal (p. 34). The paper's chamber-size result points the same way for a 435-seat House and a 100-seat Senate. It suggests that leadership confers a different structural advantage in each chamber and that minority ranking seats confer less than the 2/3 ratio implies. The pillar measures structural CU power rather than general effectiveness, so the evidence argues for chamber-specific scaling, not specific multiplier values.

bearings.paper_claim: Stage-based effectiveness is a valid construct: SLES explains about half the variance in North Carolina expert rankings (2005-2012), and lagged scores persist (rho 0.38 entered majority, 0.40 entered minority, 0.66 no change in control). Effectiveness reflects innate or cultivated lawmaking ability as well as position.
bearings.paper_location: pp. 24-25; Figures 1-2
bearings.system_side: The blend assumes 'Rank measures influence'. The live weights are Leg .45, Press .10, Inf .40, Demo .05. The brain records (run-4l, CEL LES 117-118 mean vs model score, Spearman) that LES is roughly orthogonal to the blended score and to the Leg pillar (+0.10; n not stated in the note), against a pre-registered bar of +0.30. The brain attributes this to the pillar being CU-topical by construct.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper validates general lawmaking effectiveness, not CU-specific leverage. The orthogonality result therefore does not refute the rank, but it does mean that no external effectiveness criterion currently supports the influence reading of the rank. This holds only if the CEL LES is accepted as the federal analogue of SLES, which it is: same authors, same construction.

bearings.paper_claim: Bill advancement is structurally tilted toward majority members (+0.370, 58% above the minority mean; UNSTRATIFIED pooled), chairs (+0.507 pooled; 0.609 / 0.307 by chamber), senior members (+0.032 per term) and moderates (distance from median -0.114). Minority members advance fewer bills because of their position, not only their effort.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1, pp. 25-27
bearings.system_side: The overall say-do gate requires an advancement rate of at least 20% when a member has 10 or more direct sponsored bills, and treats high introduction with low advancement as cheap talk. It is display-only and fails open. There is no adjustment for majority status, chair status or seniority.
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are state-level associations, and Volden-Wiseman report the same pattern in Congress. Because the gate is display-only, the effect is on labels, not rank. A minority member's low advancement rate should not be read as cheap talk without a within-chamber, majority-adjusted baseline.

gaps_exposed: Live Leg% (legacy mode) and Influence% (committee raw/max) pool the House and Senate in one percentile or maximum. The paper says effectiveness scores are relative to each chamber-term and should not be compared across chambers. Only the unactivated shadow normalizes within each chamber.

No component models majority versus minority status, even though the paper finds it is the largest structural driver of advancement (0.370 pooled, 58% above the minority mean). The live efficiency term and the say-do advancement threshold both absorb it unadjusted.

Score persistence depends on whether majority control changed (rho 0.38/0.40 vs 0.66). The 0.8-per-Congress decay in the shadow and in congress-activity scoring treats every prior Congress alike, whatever happened to party control.
The shadow's substantive-significance tiering, which uses CU and trade-association mention frequency, has no coding audit comparable to the paper's 49,037-bill check (95.2% correct before revision).

The live blended score has no external effectiveness validation. CEL LES is roughly orthogonal to it (+0.10), and the shadow that would bring in a stage-weighted measure is still unactivated (activation is Paul's product decision).
No ideological-distance-from-median term appears in any effectiveness or advancement measure, although moderates score higher (-0.114 per unit of distance).
flags: Pooled coefficients: the paper's Model 1.1 chair (0.507) and majority (0.370) estimates pool 97 chambers. They are quoted here with lower/upper strata (0.609/0.307; 0.362/0.387). Any downstream reuse must keep the strata or carry an UNSTRATIFIED label.

The shadow is labeled Bucchianeri/Volden/Wiseman-style in the brain, but it departs from SLES in cosponsor credit, timing decay, letters as substantive, and CU-mention significance. Citing this paper's validity checks as validation of the shadow would over-claim. Any shadow-vs-LES convergence analysis stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The paper presents associations only and calls Study 2 exploratory, with endogenous institutions (p. 34). None of its institutional coefficients should be imported as multipliers.

The paper cites network-effectiveness work (Battaglini et al. 2020; Kirkland 2011). It does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so it does not conflict with the two rejected SNA proposals.
No LDA, revolving-door or graph-rank language is involved, so D-021 and D-025 are not implicated.
paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's takeaway that effectiveness should be measured by stage progression, with LES as the criterion; he highlighted LES via Aref & Neal and Sotoudeh. It also supports his preference for observable, costly action. His recorded citations for the effectiveness shadow (Aref & Neal, Sotoudeh, Ramey) omit this paper, even though the shadow lane was commissioned in September as a Bucchianeri/Volden/Wiseman-style build. On that point his notes are stale. They also do not reflect two facts recorded in the brain: the live score is roughly orthogonal to CEL LES (+0.10), and the shadow has been built and verified but not activated. The paper gives no support to any particular pillar weights, so his position that the blend weights are untested owner policy still stands.

related.why: Sotoudeh measures cosponsorship-network influence on bill passage in the House, contrasting it with Volden-Wiseman LES. This paper supplies the stage-based LES construct that Sotoudeh contrasts with.

Both study U.S. state legislators' lawmaking behavior from state bill-sponsorship records. Fouirnaies & Hall look at effort under electoral incentives; this paper measures effectiveness and its institutional correlates.
Aref & Neal use LES-style effectiveness to characterize a hidden effective bloc. This paper supplies the measurement design and validity evidence for that kind of score.
Ramey's ceremonial-bill finding is scored in lep_criterion.py on CEL data. The commemorative tier (weight 1) of this paper's significance scheme is the same construct.
Porter maps House committee structure. This paper quantifies how chairs and committee institutions translate into lawmaking advantage, and how that varies by chamber.

backlinks.why: Brings the Volden-Wiseman effectiveness framing that Aref and Neal invoke to the state level. Relevant to whether coalition-composition effects on effectiveness generalize beyond the US House.

The text is a technical manual, so there are no statistical results, regressions or network estimates to read. Metadata hint corrected: the title, author, date and "working paper (MIT)" label match the text; no DOI is given. No Paul markup file was supplied (the task listed none), so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: No explicit research question. The document describes and documents the LobbyView database, which links congressional bill sponsorship with lobbying reports filed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995, and the API used to bulk-download it (Abstract; Section 1).
extraction.theory: No theory section. The Abstract gives the motivation only: lobbying by special interest groups matters for policymaking, and empirical studies of political representation have been limited by the difficulty of observing a direct link between politicians and interest groups.
extraction.data: Source: the universe of lobbying reports filed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 (Abstract). Units named in the text: lobbying reports, lobbying issue sections ("specific issues"), bills (ids of the form "110_HR7311", Section 5.2), firms/clients, and industries (NAICS2 groupings, Section 5.5). Sample size N: not reported. Time period: not stated as a single range; the CONGRESSES setting in general.py sets the range and its default values are not given (Section 4.1). Example years used in the text are illustrative (2002 Mattel report, 2011 filter example, 2013 Google report). Firm financials come from Compustat (Section 5.5.2), and industry codes from NAICS and SIC. The 52,418 count in Section 5.3 is a query result over all loaded reports that carry the TRADE (DOMESTIC/FOREIGN) issue; the text gives no year restriction for it.
extraction.method: Descriptive data construction, not statistical estimation. Bills in reports are found by regular-expression search for bill numbers (Section 2, step 1). The Congress is assigned by maximizing the cosine similarity between a bag-of-words vector of each candidate bill and a vector of the text around the bill mention, over the candidate Congresses (Section 2, step 2, Eq. 1). Congress numbers propagate across a report, with majority vote where bills disagree (step 3). Bill titles are matched to report text (step 4). Bill ranges are expanded (step 5). Storage uses SQLite with SQLAlchemy and Elixir, and full-text search uses Whoosh over CRS summaries and specific issues (Sections 3.1, 5.4). Herfindahl indices are computed per industry (herfindahl.py), then augmented with a trade-issue indicator and Compustat data (herfindadd.py) (Section 5.5).
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim and presents no identification strategy.
extraction.scope: Population: lobbying reports and firms/clients under the LDA (1995 onward). Institution: US Congress bills and their sponsorship. Era: post-1995 LDA filings, with the Congress range set in configuration. Stated purpose: enable systematic research on lobbying and merging with external datasets (Abstract).

summary_md:
Kim's 2018 LobbyView note is a partial technical manual, not an empirical study. It has no estimates, no N and no stated coverage window. It documents how LDA lobbying reports get linked to congressional bills. First, a regex finds bill numbers. Then each mention is assigned to a Congress by taking the argmax of cosine similarity between the candidate bill text and the text around the mention, looking back three Congresses by default; if nothing matches, the code falls back to the filing-year Congress. The Congress is then propagated across the report by majority vote, titles are matched, and close bill numbers (gap of 10 or less) are expanded into ranges. Industries are grouped by NAICS2/SIC for per-industry Herfindahl indices, with Compustat merged in. The note names one failure case: Google's 2013 report cites H.R. 2577, which is a 112th-Congress bill, so the naive filing-year rule gets it wrong. It gives no error rates for any heuristic.

This matters for Paul's lobbying lane in three ways:
1. **Every LobbyView-derived member link is a bill-roster join, not a contact record.** That backs the system's finding that the lobbied-member link is circular.
2. **Paul's own LDA rebuild uses a different bill-resolution rule than the LobbyView pipeline.** A citation without an "of 20XX" suffix binds to the filing-year Congress, which is the naive rule this paper says fails. Hyphenated ranges are not expanded. So the network.csv vintage (2000-2022) and the 2021+ rebuild are different instruments with an unmeasured seam between them.
3. **The paper uses NAICS as an industry grouping.** The system has ruled NAICS to be linkage metadata only.

None of this is a validation of anything. The heuristics' accuracy is unreported, and the argmax always returns an answer.

extraction.research_question: Can network centrality computed from co-voting records (correlations between members' voting records) identify the actual cue-provider or leader in a legislature, and in particular does a proposed absolute-value centrality measure separate cue-providers from followers and majoritarians where the traditional centrality approach cannot? (Inferred from the appendix; the main question is stated in the published article, which is not in this text.)
extraction.theory: Leader or cue-provider theory: a leader whose followers vote with her some percentage of the time (ally followers, opponent followers, or others at other rates). The appendix argues the leader should have the highest network centrality in a co-voting network built from phi correlations of voting records (lines 318-353). Majoritarians are members who vote with the majority; the traditional centrality approach can rank majoritarians above the actual cue-provider (Figure 4 text, line 303).
extraction.data: Empirical data (Table 1, line 12-120): 940 MEP observations (centrality N = 897 after network construction; left-right distance to EP median N = 868; pro/anti-EU distance to EP median N = 872). Unit is the MEP. Variables include centrality (mean .283, SD .138, range .006-.502), party leader (mean .05), committee leader (.09), EP leader (.03), coordinator (.23), reports drafted (mean 1.05), reports amended (6.73), opinions (.72), motions (6.82), speeches (29.07), questions (20.07), declarations (.58), tenure (1.58), party size (172.01), female (.30). Period of the European Parliament data is not stated in the appendix text. Simulated data (Figures 1-6, lines 289-313): 1000 simulated networks per network class (simple, moderate, complex); 1000 simulations; 100 legislators; 1000 rounds of voting in the Figure 5 runs. Figure 6 uses three parameterizations: US (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 40 allies, 40 opponents, 20 others at 50%), Supermajority (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 67 allies, 33 opponents), and EP (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 37 allies, 25 opponents, 38 others at varied rates, roughly the seven-party EP seat allotment).
extraction.method: Centrality is built from pairwise phi correlations of binary voting records (Table 1 is the 2x2 contingency table underlying phi, lines 331-341). The appendix uses an absolute-value version of this centrality, referred to as the "posterior" measure, which is compared with the traditional (signed) centrality calculation. Analytic method: Hypothesis 1 (leader centrality >= follower centrality) is proved algebraically for a three-voter legislature (leader plus two followers) with follow probabilities q2 and q3 and leader Yes-probability p; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (lines 319-345). The result is extended to n voters by a term-by-term comparison, arguing that each phi term depends only on p and the relevant follow probabilities, so it is unchanged as voters are added (lines 347-353). Simulation method: Monte Carlo generation of cueing networks in three complexity classes, computing the posterior centrality from simulated voting records and correlating it with betweenness, closeness, and weighted degree (Figure 5); and t-tests of cue-provider centrality against the maximum follower and a majoritarian across rounds of voting (Figure 6). Figures 1-4 show cue-provider centrality as a function of follow probabilities.
extraction.scope: Population: members of the European Parliament (party groups named in Table 2: EPP, EPP-ED, PES, ALDE, G/EFA, EUL/NGL, IND/DEM, UEN), plus stylized simulated legislatures (US, supermajority, and EP-style). Institution: European Parliament (empirical) and abstract legislatures (theory). Era: not stated in the appendix text. The theoretical result is stated for single-party legislatures under the stated assumptions.

summary_md:
This is the online appendix to Ringe and Wilson's paper on co-voting centrality. It holds a proof, simulations and descriptive tables from the European Parliament. The authors build a network from pairwise phi correlations of members' binary voting records. They score each member by an absolute-value (sign-blind) centrality: a member followed reliably by allies (positive phi) or reliably opposed by opponents (negative phi) both count toward that member's centrality.

**Proof.** For a single-party legislature, they show the leader's centrality is at least as high as any follower's. The condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1. The inequalities are weak (greater than or equal), although the n-voter text says "greater".

**Simulations.** There were 1,000 networks per complexity class, with 100 legislators and 1,000 voting rounds.
- The absolute-value measure separates the cue-provider from followers and from "majoritarians" (members who usually vote with the majority).
- The traditional signed measure can rank majoritarians above the true cue-provider when a third group follows at 35% (Figure 4).
- The measure correlates highly with closeness and weighted degree (no coefficient reported), but only about 0.25 with betweenness.
- Moderate and complex networks lose structure when converted to voting data.
- The authors say the results are "highly dependent on parameterization".

**Empirical side.** The data cover 897 MEPs with centrality scores (mean .283). The parliamentary term is not stated in the appendix.

**Why it matters here.**
- Melange has one co-voting layer: the signed vote backbone in the Draft Systems R script, plus its party-controlled Option C. That layer found the raw signed backbone was about 95% party, then dropped the negative side. The paper offers a mechanism for the first finding (the signed measure rewards majoritarians) and an argument against the second (negative ties carry cue-provider information).
- The paper also clarifies the June 2026 retirement of cosponsor centrality from the Influence pillar. The paper treats sign-blindness as a property of a leadership measure, not as a flaw. That supports the system's two-axis rule, which keeps influence and alignment as separate axes.
- None of this transfers directly. The evidence is analytic and simulated, with European Parliament data, and it concerns co-voting, not cosponsorship.

bearings.paper_claim: Signed (traditional) co-voting centrality cannot separate the cue-provider from majoritarians, and with a third group following at 35% it ranks majoritarians above the true cue-provider. The absolute-value measure, which credits reliable negative correlation (opponents following at 20-35%) as well as positive correlation, corrects this. Cue-provider centrality is lowest when follow probabilities are 50% and highest as they approach 0 or 1.
bearings.paper_location: Figure 4 text (line 303); Figure 3 text (line 297); Figure 1 text (line 291)
bearings.system_side: The component text says DW-NOMINATE vote edges were rejected in favour of a signed backbone. The co-voting backbone is built by R backbone::sdsm(signed=TRUE) on a member x (vote, side) bipartite graph, so the projection counts agreements (yea-yea plus nay-nay). The brain records that the raw signed backbone was about 95% party (93% of positive edges same-party, 99% of negative edges cross-party). Option C used a party-controlled null and then DROPPED the negative side, keeping only cross-party positive edges as 'Vote Affinity' (a 30% booster in the Signed Coalitions sheet). Separately, the Python signed_coalitions.py partitions the signed MENTION layer (member_references.json), not votes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper models cue-taking around a single leader in a single-party legislature, with simulated, independent follow probabilities and European Parliament data. Its target is leader identification, while the system's goal is cross-party affinity for flip targeting, so the critique of dropping negatives applies only if the layer were reused for leadership or cue detection. The paper's majoritarian mechanism plausibly explains why the raw signed backbone collapsed onto party in a two-party House. That explanation is UNVERIFIED for US data and the 119th Congress until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

The leader's centrality is >= every follower's, given only q2 < 1 and q3 < 1, so direction-blindness is a design property of a leadership measure, not a defect. The posterior measure tracks closeness and weighted degree closely but correlates only about 0.25 with betweenness.

It was retired from Influence on 2026-06-25 (AB13 0.65 -> 0) as 'direction-blind' because it raised anti-CU bill authors (Durbin, centrality 0.94, fell from rank 386 to 524 after removal). The live Influence pillar is committee-only. The system's stated rule is that rank measures influence and that stance is a separate axis.

It suggests the retirement rationale mixed the two axes: a sign-blind leadership score is legitimate on the influence axis. However, the paper never validates centrality against outcomes such as bill passage, and Sotoudeh's highlight ('not a strong indicator of bill passage') still stands. The paper also implies the 0.25 betweenness weight is the least recoverable term if the network were ever rebuilt from votes. Any revived centrality rank is a heuristic model output, never an access or influence probability (D-025).

gaps_exposed: No component computes a leadership or cue-provider score from roll-call co-voting. The roll-call ledger exists (fec/legislation/collect_official_rollcall_events.py), but nothing turns it into a co-voting network apart from the June workbook-era Draft Systems _vote_backbone.R affinity layer.

The vote-backbone affinity layer discards negative (reliable-opposition) ties. Per the paper these carry cue-provider information, so the system cannot tell a reliable cross-pressure leader from a maverick, a confound the brain itself records (the Massie/Gosar/Roy negatives).
Nothing tests whether the raw signed backbone's collapse onto party is a majoritarian artifact, as the paper's Figure 4 mechanism predicts, rather than true party cueing.

The centrality retirement was judged on CU alignment (opponents rising), not on any leadership or effectiveness criterion. No test checks whether sign-blind centrality predicts effectiveness (CEL LES, bill advancement) on the influence axis.
flags: The paper's title frames co-voting centrality as 'a measure of political influence'. If adopted, any centrality rank must be worded as a heuristic model output, never as closeness, access or an influence probability (D-025).

The paper does not argue for either REJECTED SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges, or per-edge volume normalization). Phi correlation is a per-pair standardized agreement on votes, not a reweighting of cosponsor edges, so it must not be cited as support for per-edge volume normalization.

The component description for melange-sna.signed-coalitions says 'signed backbone' (vote-based), but fec/network/signed_coalitions.py:6-8 partitions the signed mention layer (member_references.json). The vote backbone lives only in Draft Systems/_vote_backbone.R and the workbook. The component inventory conflates the two.

The empirical evidence comes from European Parliament MEPs (term not stated) and the rest is simulation. Any claim transferred to the US House or Senate is UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The proof gives weak inequalities only and is restricted to a single-party legislature.
The empirical leader ranking pools 897 MEPs across party groups. Table 2 gives within-group leaders, but the overall rank is UNSTRATIFIED across the party fault line (the top 17 are all EPP).
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation on this paper. His centrality-component position is that more research on forms of centrality is needed (Ardekani), that directionality matters (Haythornthwaite), and that eigenvector centrality is not a strong indicator of bill passage (Sotoudeh highlight). The paper partly cuts against reading 'direction-blind' as a defect: it argues that sign-blindness is what lets centrality find cue-providers, which fits the system's own influence-versus-alignment two-axis rule. It agrees with Paul's call for more centrality forms, offering co-voting absolute-value centrality as a candidate he has not considered. His notes are not stale. However, the system's June decision to keep only positive cross-party vote-backbone edges is a choice his notes never address, and this paper bears on it directly.

related.why: Both build member networks from roll-call agreement. Aref & Neal partition the signed vote network, while Ringe & Wilson score nodes by absolute-value phi centrality, and both treat negative ties as informative. The system's vote backbone was built on the Aref & Neal lineage.
This is the earlier signed co-voting coalition partition. It is the coalition-level counterpart of the paper's node-level cue-provider centrality on the same kind of data.

Sotoudeh tests cosponsorship-network centrality against bill passage and finds eigenvector centrality weak. Ringe & Wilson validate co-voting centrality only against simulated ground truth, so together they bound what centrality can and cannot show.
Both rest on cue-taking theory in legislatures. Box-Steffensmeier measures cues via Dear Colleague letters in Congress, while Ringe & Wilson infer the cue-provider from voting correlations.
Both are roll-call methods. NOMINATE scales ideology, while Ringe & Wilson extract leadership centrality from the same binary vote matrix. The system rejected DW-NOMINATE vote edges.

Both treat network centrality as pricing a legislator's influence. Battaglini & Patacchini derive Katz-Bonacich centrality theoretically (the system's kb_benchmark), while Ringe & Wilson give a co-voting measure that recovers degree and closeness well.

backlinks.why: Ringe et al. propose co-voting centrality as a measure of political influence. Azaiez states that centrality measures embeddedness and not influence directly.
It also derives member structure from House roll-call voting, as a co-voting network centrality rather than an SVD of the vote matrix.

This is the same lead author's co-voting network centrality work on the European Parliament. It uses the same co-voting outcome, but as a centrality measure where this paper uses it as a dyadic outcome.
Ringe et al. treat network centrality as a measure of political influence. Their work is a contrast case for whether a centrality ranking stands for real power, which this paper simply assumes.

summary_md:
An unsigned internal memo dated 12/10/2025. Names are redacted and it is not peer-reviewed. It profiles federal political giving by the top 10 firms by revenue in four industries: life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions and commercial banking. It splits that giving across CEOs, other executives, company PACs, trade associations (ACLI, ACU, ABA) and the four largest Super PACs. Its headline claim is that firms push political spending onto executives and adjust their giving to executive-branch scrutiny "regardless of party". The evidence is per-industry dollar averages, which carry no cycle years, source or N, plus news-driven case stories: Bank of America after the DOJ probe, JPMorgan's PAC memos, and the Schwab charity fund. There is no comparison group and no test. The memo reports its own ranking contradictions, and it uses "dark money" to mean Super PAC money.

For Paul's systems the memo is a descriptive input, not evidence. Its unit of analysis is the same one Mentat's spending-statistics sheet already builds. That sheet has role tiers (Chief, Middle Management, Employee, Corporate) and channel columns (Super PAC, Company PAC, Trade Association, Candidate, Company PAC to Super PAC, each with a partisan split). Mentat also ingests a "Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx" template. The memo may therefore come from the same product line, and if it does it is not an independent check. Two parts are useful. First, the bank, mutual-fund and CU stories show giving moving into channels that per-member models never see: trade associations, Super PACs, and family or charity vehicles. That bears on how Melange's flip model measures competitor money. Second, its partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore whether the money supported or opposed a candidate, which Mentat already separates. Every figure in the memo should be treated as UNVERIFIED, with no window or denominator.

bearings.paper_claim: Bank CEOs give little directly to candidates (several give nothing, e.g. Moynihan, Masrani). Bank money flows through company PACs and the ABA (cyclical average $2,402,499). Mutual-fund money is said to be 'channeled into Super PACs' (industry PACs about $13M cumulative versus about $261M annual average at the four biggest Super PACs). CU giving runs through ACU coordination, with $0 reported to the four biggest Super PACs.

Trade-association dollars, Super PAC independent expenditures for or against a member, and executives' individual giving never enter a or b. If the memo's channel picture holds, the b-term understates bank and fund pressure exactly where those industries avoid direct giving.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This carries over only as a structural caution. The memo's dollar figures have no stated source, cycle window or N, and some may be industry totals rather than per-member amounts. It shows no member-level allocation, so it cannot recalibrate WM or HALFF. Before any engine change, Mentat's own Super PAC and trade-association columns would need to be mapped to members.

gaps_exposed: Melange's flip and break-even money legs see only direct PAC-to-member dollars (cu, banks + finserv). Trade-association and Super PAC independent-expenditure money targeted at a member is absent, and the memo argues those are the main bank and mutual-fund channels.

Mentat has no linkage from roster executives to their personal or charitable vehicles (foundations, donor-advised funds, family entities). Giving that an executive redirects off the employer field goes unattributed.
No study variable captures executive-branch enforcement or scrutiny events (DOJ probes, executive orders). The sector-growth SHIFT tests cover congressional control only.

No figure for within-industry volatility of giving by channel. The memo calls mutual funds the most volatile, which bears on forecast interval width, but the forecast reports no per-industry dispersion.
flags: UNVERIFIED (DE-062): every dollar figure in the memo lacks a source, cycle window, N and denominator, which breaks the rule that every figure names its window and denominator. Quote none of them without that label.

The memo may not be independent of the system. Its channel and role layout matches Mentat's spending-statistics sheet (report.R:64-80), and Mentat ingests a 'Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx' template (ingest.R:1294). If it was built from Mentat output, it cannot serve as a second path that reproduces Mentat.
Terminology conflict: the memo calls Super PAC donations 'dark money'. Mentat keeps Super PAC money (FEC-disclosed) separate from 501(c) and 527 money. Do not import the memo's wording.

The memo's partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore support/oppose direction, and the brain records that 89% of beneficiary dollars were oppose-coded. 'GOP-aligned' destinations do not equal pro-GOP spending.

The causal claim (executive-branch pressure drives giving 'regardless of party') rests on narrative and timing. It sits uneasily with the memo's own GOP-tilted mutual-fund finding, and its ranking contradictions are unreconciled (bank CEO $16,781 called 1st, below the mutual-fund CEO's $17,882).
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this memo. It loosely agrees with his reading of strategic, cycle-aware giving (Bacik: more money in election years; Furnas: party-tied firms lose when that party loses). It also agrees with his wish to map rival industries (banks and funds against CUs). But it supplies only industry averages and anecdotes, with no member-level allocation. It cannot answer his 'conflicting industries' note for the industry boards or the flip model. The system's own SHIFT result found no stable partisan shift with expected control. That cuts against generalizing the memo's 'adapt to whoever holds power' story, though the memo concerns the executive branch, which SHIFT does not test. If Paul or his team wrote this memo, its framing of channel substitution is now better covered by Mentat's role and channel columns and the support/oppose partition than the memo's own figures. The memo should be read as a framing document, not as evidence.

related.why: Cross-industry finance and lobbying report under Paul's name on the same subject (industry political spending across finance sectors). It may share data lineage with this memo; that is unverified because this memo's names are redacted.

Furnas et al. show low overlap between organizations' lobbying and PAC spending. That supports the memo's premise that money moves across separate channels, and warns against treating any single channel as an industry's total effort.
Irvin investigates real dark money (nonprofit 501(c) advocacy). That corrects the memo's use of 'dark money' for disclosed Super PAC donations.
Couch et al. model a dark-money transfer network. That is the network view the memo's Super PAC 'reservoir' claim would need, and it parallels Mentat's PAC transfer graph.
Kim et al. link firm-level donations to lobbying using executive and employee giving matched to firms. That is the rigorous version of the memo's executive-offloading measurement.

authors: Eric Merkley (Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy, University of Toronto)
Dominik A. Stecula (Annenberg Public Policy Center, University of Pennsylvania; Simon Fraser University)
extraction.venue: British Journal of Political Science (marked "Forthcoming" in the PDF; no volume, issue or DOI given)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1,068 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\049ac0d19237.txt (title, abstract, introduction, theory, data and methods, aggregate results, experiment, discussion, references). The supplementary information (sections A-B, Tables C/D/E, Figures C1-C2, E1-E2) is referenced but not in the file, so it was not evaluated. Annotation file C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\049ac0d19237.json read in full: 51 Highlight items, no sticky notes, every note field empty. Metadata hint corrected: authors are Merkley and Stecula; the PDF gives no year or DOI.
extraction.research_question: Does out-group cueing from Democratic elites, delivered through news coverage, drive the rise of climate skepticism in the US public, especially among Republicans, and can that effect be shown to be causal rather than a by-product of confounders?
extraction.theory: Elite cueing and out-group backlash. Partisans use party elites as cognitive shortcuts and affective anchors (Cohen 2003; Kam 2005; Lenz 2012; Lodge and Taber 2013). Out-group cues can repel rather than persuade partisans, plausibly via affective polarization (Iyengar et al. 2012). The authors contrast this with motivated-reasoning and ideology accounts, which they say cannot easily explain the over-time dynamics, since Republicans once matched Democrats on climate beliefs. News media carry elite cues to the mass public (pp. 2-6). Hypotheses: H1, Democratic elite cues lead aggregate skepticism; H2, a positive contemporaneous correlation holds after controls; H3, exposure to a Democratic cue raises skepticism among Republicans (pp. 5-8).
extraction.data: Aggregate opinion: about 172 Roper Center poll questions (the abstract says "nearly 200 polls") combined into a latent skepticism index. Quarterly 2001-2014 (N=55 in Table 2 Model 1; N=54 for the Republican series) and annual 1986-2014 (N=28). Republican-only series is the Partisan Climate Change Threat Index of Carmichael and Brulle, reverse-coded (correlation 0.48 with the authors' quarterly series). News: climate coverage in the New York Times and Washington Post (LexisNexis), with 1,000+ articles hand-screened for relevance. Validation: 700 party-referencing articles (about 80% contain a cue); 3,000 articles coded for stance (97% of Democratic-cue articles fully pro-consensus); 2,179 newspaper articles coded for economic-cost and uncertainty frames (classifier training sets of 1,878 and 1,179). Experiment: MTurk, 2019, N=2,970 analysed (condition sizes 471-534), with 85% passing screeners and 130 (4%) dropped for failing both (p. 19 and fn 10).
extraction.method: Text-as-data pipeline: Lexicoder plus a custom dictionary of party names, office titles and leaders to flag elite cues. Share of articles with Democratic cues and Republican cues. Republican cue measure is the cue share multiplied by the share of hostile Republican messages (validated against LCV scores, r=0.72). Frames via SVM (80% accuracy for cost frames, recall 0.76 and precision 0.80; 77% accuracy for uncertainty frames, recall 0.70 and precision 0.68). Time series: reduced-form VAR with lags up to four quarters (higher lag chosen when tests disagree; stability checked) and Granger causality tests, with controls for NOAA climate index, oil prices, unemployment and quarter dummies (pp. 11-13). Contemporaneous models: lagged-dependent-variable OLS with robust SEs (Eq. 1), controls for Republican cues, uncertainty and cost frames, salience (NYT plus WaPo volume), climate, oil, unemployment (Table 2). Experiment: OLS (Eq. 2) interacting five treatment dummies (Democratic cue; opposing GOP cue; polarized cues; supporting GOP cue; consensus cues) with 7-point partisanship and with controls (trust in scientists, political interest) and their interactions with treatment. Outcome is a 7-point agree/disagree item on human-caused warming, rescaled 0-1 (pp. 18-21).
extraction.identification: Time series: Granger tests establish temporal precedence only, and the authors state the design is not causal (pp. 6, 12, 17). Contemporaneous models add controls for in-group cues, frames, salience, and lagged skepticism, but remain observational. Experiment: random assignment to six conditions (control; Democratic cue; opposing GOP cue; polarized; supporting GOP cue; consensus), so the cue effect is identified within the randomized conditions. Partisanship is not randomized and enters as a moderator (p. 19). The effects reported are conditional on strong partisanship. Effects are estimated through the PID-by-treatment interaction, not a simple randomized mean difference.
extraction.scope: Population: US public (aggregate polls) and a US online MTurk sample (2019) that the authors say matches the public on gender, race, partisanship and ideology but skews younger, wealthier and more educated (p. 18). Institution: national newspaper coverage (NYT and WaPo) only. Era: 1986-2014 for annual opinion and 2001-2014 for quarterly series; experiment in 2019. Issue: climate change science and mitigation.

limitations: VAR and Granger analyses cannot speak to contemporaneous relationships or causality; authors say so (pp. 6, 12, 16).
Aggregate evidence is described as only suggestive; unmeasured confounders over time remain (p. 17).
Results are sensitive to lag length; the authors pick the higher lag when tests disagree and note the sensitivity (fn 6, p. 12).
Small time series (N=28 annual, 54-55 quarterly) with many controls.
Cue measure is a share of articles from dictionary-based classification, not message volume; volume robustness is only in supplementary Table D1 (p. 10).

Republican hostility measure is a composite built from a 3,000-article coding and an LCV correlation (0.72); the authors call the stance indicator valid but it is not directly measured for every period (pp. 10-11).
Only NYT and WaPo are used; the authors acknowledge partisan online and social media are excluded (fn 3, p. 9).
Inconsistent counts: the abstract says nearly 200 polls, the body uses 172 poll questions (p. 8). The abstract says about 3,000 respondents; 2,970 were analysed.
Experimental sample is MTurk, skewing younger, wealthier and more educated; screeners address bot and VPN concerns (pp. 18-19, fn 10).
Partisanship is not randomized; treatment effects are moderated by PID, which may carry confounding (p. 19).
No effect among Democrats, possibly from a ceiling effect (p. 22).
Treatments are thin and the outcome is a single 7-point item (pp. 18-21).
Consensus cue did not depolarize; the authors suggest a stronger treatment from respected Republicans may be needed (p. 23).
Table 2 layout is hard to read: the text reports Model 1 Republican cues as non-significant, while the table marks Dem cues only with stars; p-values are reported as approximate (p~).

summary_md:
Merkley and Stecula ask whether climate skepticism in the US public grew because people reacted against Democratic elites, with news coverage carrying those cues. They combine three methods. First, a Lexicoder dictionary flags party cues in NYT and WaPo climate coverage. Second, they run time-series models on a latent skepticism index built from about 172 poll questions. Third, they run a 2019 MTurk experiment with N=2,970.

In the time series, the share of articles carrying Democratic cues Granger-causes skepticism, both in the aggregate (chi2 6.96, p=0.01) and among Republicans (chi2 7.35, p=0.03). The reverse direction does not hold. Republican cues have no aggregate effect (p=0.94). In the experiment, a single Democratic cue moves strong Republicans +0.06 toward skepticism on a 0-1 scale (about 0.2 SD). A polarized cue, Democrats for and Republicans against, moves them +0.09. A consensus cue, with Republicans joining Democrats, produces no movement and does not depolarize. More coverage alone, with cues held fixed, goes with lower Republican skepticism (-0.4 SD per +100 articles a quarter). The Granger tests show only which series moves first, not causation. The causal evidence is one MTurk experiment on mass partisans, not legislators.

For Melange, the paper's value is about direction. An out-party cue is not a weaker positive cue. Among mass partisans it pushes the other way. Three parts of the engine encode out-party cues differently:
- The cascade kernel's cpf_pressure gives an out-party source 0.5x pull, a weaker push in the same direction.
- The LT-priming cross-cue is clamped at 0 and never goes negative.
- The salience shock already has a Retreat regime that moves out-partisans -1, but its Rally regime still gives bridge-builders +0.5. The paper's consensus condition found no movement at all.

The paper does not supply a legislator-level backfire magnitude. Every transfer runs from the mass public to members of Congress and from climate to credit-union issues, so any recalibration is UNVERIFIED and remains Paul's decision.

bearings.paper_claim: A polarized cue (Democrats for, Republicans against) moves strong Republicans +0.09 on a 0-1 scale (about 0.3 SD, p~0.002), the largest effect. A single Democratic cue moves them +0.06 (p~0.03). A consensus cue (Democrats plus supportive Republicans) produces no significant movement and no depolarization. In observational data, coverage volume with cues held fixed goes with LOWER Republican skepticism (-0.4 SD per +100 articles a quarter, p~0.03), so salience by itself is not what polarizes. Who is attributed the message is.
bearings.paper_location: Experimental results, Figure 3 Panels A-C, pp. 20-21; Table 2 Model 3, p. 17; discussion pp. 22-23
bearings.system_side: Going public is modelled as three regimes. Retreat moves co-partisans +1 and out-partisans -1, which matches the paper's polarized-cue backlash. Rally moves out-partisans +0.5 when bpf >= 0.30, which this paper's consensus null does not support. The regime probabilities p and q come from the current D-R tier gap z, a snapshot that the campaign itself never changes, and the actor's party defaults to R in the advisory.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as a direction-of-effect prior. The paper studies mass partisans responding to elite cues in national newspapers on climate, an issue with a large partisan gap; the engine moves legislators' stance tiers on credit-union issues. The rally result is a single thin MTurk treatment, so it weakens the case for out-partisan rally movement but does not refute it. The Granger evidence that Democratic cues come before Republican skepticism suggests z is endogenous to going public, but the paper estimates nothing that could calibrate that effect.

Experiment: strong Republicans +0.06 toward skepticism (about 0.2 SD, p~0.03), with a PID interaction p~0.05. bearings.system_side: The Bakker cross-cue factor passes a cross-party pro-cue through sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), so a non-bridge out-party cue falls to about 0. It is clamped at 0 and never goes negative, and the code comment says 'backfire magnitude not invented'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper backs the claim that out-party cues do not persuade, and it suggests the true sign can be negative. Its +0.06 effect is measured on mass Republicans and a single climate item, not on legislators reading cosponsorship signals. It therefore cannot justify a negative magnitude for the priming term. Keeping the 0 clamp remains defensible.

On issues as polarized as climate in the mass public, it puts the out-partisan sign at or below zero, not 0.5. The kernel runs on legislator cosponsorship ties, where out-party cosponsorship is an observed behaviour, not a cue, so transfer is weak. The paper gives no support for the 1.7/0.5 ratio itself.

They validate it against hand coding of 700 articles (about 80% of flagged articles contain a real cue). Stance is hand-coded separately (97% of Democratic-cue articles fully pro-consensus), and frames come from SVMs (77-80% accuracy).

gaps_exposed: The engine never lets a source's party identity produce a negative cue. The cascade kernel, LT priming and the rally regime all keep out-party influence at zero or above. The only negative out-party movement is the salience shock's Retreat and Backfire regimes, and it never feeds the cascade kernel.

The salience shock takes partisan polarization (z) as a fixed snapshot of the stance matrix. Nothing models a CU campaign led by one party creating or widening the partisan gap over later quarters, which is the dynamic the Granger results describe.

Message attribution, meaning which party's elites are seen as owning a CU issue in press and news, is not measured. The frame-alignment and press layers measure duplication and stance, not attribution of party cues in third-party coverage.
The salience shock has no consensus regime. The paper's consensus condition (both parties supportive) is a distinct case with a null effect, not a rally that moves out-partisans +0.5.
flags: The paper's aggregate contemporaneous coefficient (0.02, p~0.07 quarterly; p~0.09 annual) pools Democrats and Republicans across the partisan fault line the paper is about. If quoted, label it UNSTRATIFIED and pair it with the Republican-only Model 3 (0.03, p<0.01, N=54, quarterly 2001-2014).
The Granger results depend on lag choice (the authors take the higher lag when tests disagree, fn 6). Quote them as evidence of which series moves first, never as causal.

Any proposal to give out-partisan pressure a negative sign, or to set a backfire magnitude in lt_priming, from the +0.06 or +0.09 MTurk effects would be new agent analysis, UNVERIFIED (DE-062). Those effects are mass-public climate effects and say nothing about legislators.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025. The paper argues for neither dropping cosponsorship edges nor per-edge volume normalization.
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights match the paper's core claim (Democratic cues, Republican backlash, consensus cues fail). His component notes list Merkley and Stecula as support for treating party as a filter on receptiveness (cascade kernel) and as a companion to Noble and Turner (salience shock). The evidence agrees on direction but is stronger than the system as built. The paper finds that out-party cues backfire. In the code, out-party influence is attenuated but positive in cpf_pressure and the rally regime, and clamped at 0 in LT priming. So Paul's note is consistent with the system but understates the gap: the system handles backfire only through the salience shock's Retreat and Backfire regimes. His highlight of the Lexicoder method under lsd-tone is a loose fit. The paper used Lexicoder to detect party actors, not to measure tone, so it does not validate the LSD intensity the system uses. His closing highlights on cross-partisan elite consensus are tempered by the paper's own null for the consensus condition.

related.why: Noble and Turner supply the rally, retreat and backfire structure the salience shock implements. Merkley and Stecula give mass-public experimental evidence that the out-partisan retreat direction is real, and that a consensus or rally cue does not move out-partisans.

Bakker et al. is the cited basis for the LT-priming cross-cue clamp, which treats out-party cues as having null-to-backfire effects. Merkley and Stecula independently find backfire from out-party cues, on climate and in a news setting.

Both papers study cue-taking. Box-Steffensmeier et al. look at legislators taking cues from interest-group Dear Colleague letters. Merkley and Stecula look at the mass public taking cues from party elites in the news. Together they mark the boundary between legislator and voter evidence for the cue parameters.

Both rely on dictionaries for political text. Rice and Zorn argue that general-purpose sentiment dictionaries need adaptation to specialized vocabularies, which bears on applying LSD2015 to congressional releases. Merkley and Stecula use Lexicoder only with a custom dictionary validated against hand coding.

Haselmayer and Jenny also pair dictionary-based measurement of political communication with human validation (crowdcoding). That is the validation step the paper models and the system's LSD tone layer lacks.
